# Cancer

::: {.callout-warning}
## First draft
Written from `research/06-cancer.yml` and not yet reviewed by a second reader.
:::

Cancer transcriptomes are usually read for which genes went up and which went
down. A large fraction of what changes in a tumour does not move a gene total
at all, and this chapter is about that fraction and about how much of it holds
up.

## Changes a gene-level analysis retires {#sec-invisible-switches}

Treatment-naive oesophageal tissue was scored for isoform switches during
progression from low-grade to high-grade Barrett's dysplasia. Between 42 and 46
per cent of the genes called that way showed no significant difference in total
gene-level expression between the same two conditions [@zhang2022esophageal].

A reanalysis of twelve TCGA cancer types using differential transcript usage, in
the sense of @sec-dtu, found that roughly a quarter of the tumour-side
transcripts that changed in usage were not themselves called differentially
expressed. Only a few per cent of the normal-side transcripts behaved that way
[@dolgalev2023switching]. That figure counts transcripts and the one above
counts genes, so the two do not combine.

Among the isoform pairs distinguishing basal-like from luminal breast tumours
in TCGA, 49 of 229 pairs showed no accompanying difference in gene-level
expression, so splicing was the only signal available for those genes
[@zhao2016switching].

The cleanest version is an engineered one. In an isogenic SRSF2 P95H
erythroleukaemia model, over a thousand significant alternative splicing events
were called, two thirds of them cassette exons, while overall gene expression
between mutant and wild-type cells barely moved [@liang2018srsf2].

### Two reasons to discount part of that

Not every called switch is an exchange of one isoform for another. In about half
of the switches that were not concordant in usage and expression, one partner
transcript did not change expression at all. Those authors say that makes the
event better described as a single-transcript expression change
[@dolgalev2023switching].

Relative transcript measurements also inherit every coverage bias in the
library. In one breast cancer cohort an initial 2,110 inversely correlated
isoform pairs collapsed to 470 once RNA integrity number was modelled as a
covariate, because degraded RNA inflates the apparent abundance of short
isoforms [@zhao2016switching]. Nearly four in five of those pairs were a
property of the samples.

## Splicing factor mutations {#sec-splicing-factors}

SF3B1 is the single most commonly mutated gene in myelodysplastic syndromes,
carried by roughly a fifth to somewhat over a quarter of all patients
[@dolatshad2016abcb7].

The ring-sideroblast phenotype traces to one splicing lesion. A cryptic 3'
splice site inserts 21 intronic bases into the iron transporter ABCB7
transcript, creating a premature stop codon. The aberrant transcript was
detected in every SF3B1-mutant patient sample tested, and in none of the
wild-type or healthy controls [@dolatshad2016abcb7].

The genome-wide picture is larger than one gene. Mutant SF3B1 activates several
hundred novel 3' splice sites, with closely matched counts in an engineered
K700E cell line and in primary MDS samples [@kesarwani2017cryptic]. One
mechanistic account holds that those cryptic sites are normally base-paired
inside RNA secondary structure and therefore invisible to the scanning
spliceosome, and the reduced-accessibility signature held in an independent CLL
cohort [@kesarwani2017cryptic].

How mutant SF3B1 actually chooses its cryptic sites is contested. Those same
authors count three published and mutually incompatible mechanistic models
[@kesarwani2017cryptic], none of which should be presented as settled.

### U2AF1 and a changed preference at one position

U2AF1 is mutated in only a few per cent of lung adenocarcinomas and acute
myeloid leukaemias in TCGA. Those few cases carry hundreds of
mutation-associated splicing changes [@brooks2014u2af1].

The mechanism is a shift in what the spliceosome tolerates three bases before
the intron-exon boundary. In HeLa cells expressing the S34F mutant, 57 per cent
of competing CAG-versus-TAG 3' splice site pairs shifted, against 36 per cent
with a wild-type construct [@brooks2014u2af1].

The rule is a preference, and the same authors note that many UAG 3' splice
sites were unaffected, and that nonsense-mediated decay of aberrant products
could make affected sites look unaffected [@brooks2014u2af1].

### SRSF2 and a re-weighted enhancer code

The SRSF2 P95 hotspot works by re-weighting an exonic splicing enhancer code
rather than by abolishing binding. The mutant RNA-binding domain binds the CCNG
motif with three- to four-fold higher affinity than GGNG, where the wild-type
domain treats the two about equally [@liang2018srsf2]. One changed binding
preference is enough to redistribute splicing across the transcriptome.

Reproducibility across SRSF2 studies is a problem. When nine published RNA-seq
datasets were overlapped at the level of differentially spliced gene lists, not
a single gene appeared in all nine, and only 446 genes recurred in three or
more [@liang2018srsf2].

### ZRSR2 and the other spliceosome

ZRSR2 mutations act on the minor spliceosome. In primary MDS marrow, more than
a third of all U12-type introns were significantly more retained in
ZRSR2-mutant patients than in spliceosome-wild-type ones [@inoue2021minor].

The four MDS splicing factor genes are not interchangeable, and the clearest
evidence is that their mouse models disagree in direction. Zrsr2 deletion
enhanced haematopoietic stem cell self-renewal, whereas published hotspot
knock-ins of Sf3b1, Srsf2 and U2af1 all impaired it under comparable
transplantation assays [@inoue2021minor].

Their target sets differ as well as their phenotypes. Mis-splicing of the kinase
MAP3K7 is specific to SF3B1 among the spliceosome genes. The same isogenic K562
panel showed extensive cryptic 3' splice site use in the SF3B1 mutant and not in
SRSF2- or U2AF1-mutant cells [@lieu2021map3k7]. Even that case is partial,
since its authors claim the misspliced kinase accounts only partly for the
severe anaemia of SF3B1-mutant MDS, and explicitly not for ring sideroblast
formation [@lieu2021map3k7].

## Isoform-level inactivation that exome sequencing cannot see {#sec-lztr1}

The tumour suppressor LZTR1 is inactivated post-transcriptionally far more
often than by coding mutation. Retention of its single minor intron exceeded
the level seen in any matched normal tissue in 11.1 per cent of TCGA tumour
samples, across nearly all cancer types profiled [@inoue2021minor].

A gene can be functionally lost in a tenth of tumours with nothing in the exome
to show for it.

## Silent mutations that are not silent {#sec-silent}

How often an exonic point mutation disrupts splicing is contested. The figures
in circulation range from a quarter to over three quarters of exonic mutations,
a disagreement of more than threefold, so no single headline fraction in this
area should be quoted as settled [@hurst2017depletion].

Selection inside tumours leaves a measurable trace. Across 15 TCGA cancer
types, synonymous mutation density was about 17 per cent lower in the
splicing-regulatory flanks of exons than in exon cores. The depletion was
absent in tumour suppressors, where losing function is advantageous
[@hurst2017depletion].

A pan-cancer screen of 8,320 exomes
across 22 tumour types nominated 22,948 synonymous single-nucleotide variants as
post-transcriptionally consequential, spread over 2,042 genes
[@teng2020synonymous].

A synonymous c.936T>G change in
BAP1 exon
11 of a clear-cell renal carcinoma caused exon skipping and loss of BAP1
protein. The patient died at 56 months, against a TCGA median of 117 months for
the group her exome had placed her in [@niersch2021bap1]. That report also
cites an earlier pan-cancer estimate putting synonymous changes at roughly 6 to
8 per cent of single-nucleotide driver mutations in oncogenes, secondhand
[@niersch2021bap1]. The primary analysis should be read before that figure is
used.

## Isoform-defined drug targets {#sec-drug-targets}

Two cases show an isoform, rather than a gene, defining the target.

MET exon 14 skipping is reached by structurally diverse DNA lesions converging
on one RNA outcome. The underlying mutations sat mostly at the splice donor side
of exon 14, at 57 per cent, or the acceptor side, at 25 per cent. In the phase 1
expansion cohort, crizotinib produced a confirmed objective response in 32 per
cent of 65 evaluable patients. That is short of the 60 to 80 per cent seen with
matched therapy for other lung cancer drivers [@drilon2020met].

AR-V7 is the opposite shape of problem, an isoform that therapy creates.
Immunohistochemistry across hundreds of prostate specimens found AR-V7 protein
in under one per cent of untreated primary tumours, and in about three quarters
of samples taken after androgen deprivation. The share rose further after
abiraterone or enzalutamide [@sharp2019arv7]. The receptor form that dominates
after treatment was almost absent before it.

## Neoantigens, and how much survives a wider reference {#sec-neoantigens}

Aberrant junctions dwarf point mutations as a source of recurrent, shareable
tumour antigens. Across 8,705 TCGA tumours about 251,000 tumour-enriched
junctions were found, roughly 18,000 of them present in at least 100 samples.
Only 13 somatic point mutations reached that same recurrence threshold
[@kahles2018splicing].

![Left: how many events of each kind are shared across tumours, on a log axis
because the two differ by more than three orders of magnitude. Right: what
happens to the same junctions when the normal reference is widened beyond
tissue-matched samples.](../figures/neoantigen-recurrence.svg){#fig-neoantigen width=100%}

The same analysis cautions against reading all of that as oncogenic.
Tumour-enriched junctions were not enriched in the cancer gene census, which
those authors take as evidence that much of the extra splicing diversity is
passenger noise from degraded splicing fidelity [@kahles2018splicing].

The tumour-specificity itself does not survive a wider comparison. Averaged over
cancer types, 80.6 per cent of junctions called cancer-specific against
tissue-matched normals turn up in other adult non-cancer tissues. A further
share of those absent from all adult normals appear in developmental samples
[@david2020junctions]. The choice of normal comparison sets most of that number.

The functional evidence has been taken as far as T cell receptors. Clones
reactive to aberrant GNAS and RPL22 junctions were isolated and killed tumour
cells. Naturally occurring reactivity in patients was detected in only one of
three glioma patients tested [@kwok2025public], so the mechanism works while the
in-patient evidence stays thin.

## Therapeutics {#sec-cancer-therapeutics}

The SRSF2 motif switch connects to a named target exon. The poison exon of EZH2
contains three copies of the CCWG motif that mutant SRSF2 prefers, and none of
the GGWG motif the wild-type protein prefers. Blocking that exon with antisense
oligonucleotides was tested as a way to restore EZH2 protein in SRSF2-mutant
cancer cells [@islam2026ezh2]. The whole therapeutic logic fits inside one
exon's worth of sequence.

Modulating the spliceosome itself is less targeted than it sounds. The
SF3B1-directed compound H3B-8800 bound SF3b complexes containing wild-type or
mutant SF3B1 and altered splicing similarly in both, yet killed SF3B1- or
SRSF2-mutant cells preferentially. Those authors attribute the selectivity to
those cells' dependence on normal expression of spliceosome genes rather than
to differential drug binding [@seiler2016h3b8800].

The clinical result is the counterweight to everything above. In the phase 1
dose-expansion cohorts in transfusion-dependent SF3B1-mutant lower-risk MDS, of
7 and 36 patients, only two patients in each reached even one interval of
eight-week red cell transfusion independence. The investigators concluded the
drug was insufficiently effective at the doses tested
[@h3b8800phase1lrmds2025].

A mechanism can be correct, specific and well characterised, and still not
yield a drug. For therapy that works by modulating splicing, the isoform-level
view of cancer has changed what counts as a driver without yet changing what
counts as a treatment.

Aiming a drug at one isoform directly is a different proposition, and it has
already succeeded, as @sec-isoform-selective describes.
